title: How Alcohol Is Metabolized: The Liver Pathway, Step by Step
excerpt: How your body breaks down alcohol: the two liver enzymes that turn it into acetaldehyde and then acetate, how fast it happens, what affects it, and why some people flush.
metaDescription: How alcohol is metabolized: the liver enzymes that turn it into acetaldehyde and acetate, how fast it clears, what affects it, and why some people flush.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** your body treats alcohol as a toxin to be cleared, and your liver does almost all of the work. In two main steps, liver enzymes turn alcohol (ethanol) into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic and short-lived chemical, and then into **acetate**, a harmless substance that the rest of your body breaks down into carbon dioxide and water. Only a small share of what you drink, usually under 10%, leaves your body unchanged through your breath, urine, and sweat. The liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult, and nothing you can buy makes that pace meaningfully faster.

That one fact explains most of what people notice about drinking. It explains why drinks "stack up" when you have them faster than one an hour, why coffee and cold showers don't sober you up, why some people turn red after a single beer, and why heavy regular drinking slowly changes how the liver works. This guide walks through each step in plain words, what affects it, and what it means for you on a normal night out.

> **This is general education, not medical advice.** If you're worried about how alcohol affects you, take regular medication, or have a liver condition, talk to your doctor or pharmacist. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) right away** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and the body cannot clear alcohol fast enough to fix it on its own. Don't let them "sleep it off."

## Alcohol Metabolism in One Picture

Here is the whole journey, from glass to exhaled breath:

1. **You drink.** Ethanol is a small molecule that dissolves in both water and fat, so it moves easily through your body.
2. **You absorb it.** A little is absorbed in the stomach, but most is absorbed in the first part of the small intestine. From there it travels in the blood straight to the liver.
3. **The liver gets first pick.** Some alcohol is broken down on this first pass through the stomach lining and liver. The rest flows into your general bloodstream and spreads into every tissue that contains water, including your brain. That's when you feel it.
4. **Step one: alcohol becomes acetaldehyde.** An enzyme called **alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)** strips hydrogen off the ethanol molecule. The result is acetaldehyde.
5. **Step two: acetaldehyde becomes acetate.** A second enzyme, **aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)**, mainly a version called **ALDH2**, converts acetaldehyde into acetate.
6. **Acetate leaves the liver.** Acetate travels in the blood to muscles, the heart, and the brain, where it's burned for energy and ends up as carbon dioxide and water.
7. **A small amount escapes unchanged.** A few percent of the alcohol is breathed out, passed in urine, or lost in sweat. This tiny exhaled fraction is what a breathalyzer measures.

Everything else in this article is detail on those seven points.

## Where Is Alcohol Metabolized?

**Mostly in the liver.** The liver holds the largest supply of the enzymes that break alcohol down, and it is the first organ that absorbed alcohol reaches. Most estimates put the liver's share at roughly 90% or more of the alcohol that gets metabolized.

**A little in the stomach.** The stomach lining has its own alcohol dehydrogenase and breaks down a small portion of alcohol before it's absorbed. This is part of what's called **first-pass metabolism**. Food keeps alcohol in the stomach longer, which gives these enzymes more time and slows how quickly alcohol reaches the bloodstream. On average, women have less of this stomach enzyme activity than men, which is one of several reasons the same drink tends to produce a higher blood alcohol level in women.

**Small amounts elsewhere.** Other tissues, including the brain, have some ability to process alcohol through minor pathways, but they handle a very small share.

**Not metabolized at all: the part you breathe, sweat, and pee out.** A small fraction, usually cited as somewhere between 2% and 10%, leaves the body unchanged. Breath alcohol tests work because alcohol in your blood passes into the air in your lungs in a predictable ratio. This also explains "alcohol breath" the next morning. It isn't only from your mouth; it's coming up from your bloodstream.

If you want a deeper look at absorption speed, peak levels, and how drinks move through the body over time, our [alcohol pharmacokinetics guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-pharmacokinetics-advanced-absorption-science-2025) covers that side in detail. This article focuses on the breakdown itself.

## Step One: Alcohol Dehydrogenase Turns Ethanol Into Acetaldehyde

Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) is a family of enzymes, mostly found in the liver. Its job is to pull two hydrogen atoms off ethanol. Those hydrogens are handed to a helper molecule called **NAD+**, which becomes **NADH** in the process. The leftover molecule is acetaldehyde.

Two things about this step matter in everyday life.

**It has a speed limit.** Your liver has only so much ADH and only so much NAD+ ready at any moment. Once you've had more than a drink or so, the enzyme is working close to its maximum rate. Scientists describe this as **zero-order elimination**: the body removes a roughly fixed *amount* of alcohol per hour, not a fixed *percentage*. That's very different from most medicines, and it's why drinking faster than your liver can keep up makes your blood alcohol climb steadily. Five drinks in two hours doesn't get cleared any faster than five drinks spread across five hours. It just piles up first.

**It shifts the liver's chemistry.** Every alcohol molecule processed by ADH, and then again by ALDH, turns NAD+ into NADH. During heavy drinking, the liver ends up with too much NADH and too little NAD+. That imbalance has knock-on effects:

- **It slows sugar production.** The liver normally makes glucose to keep your blood sugar steady, especially overnight. A high NADH level interferes with that. This is one reason heavy drinking, particularly on an empty stomach, can cause low blood sugar, which contributes to shakiness, weakness, and fogginess the next day.
- **It encourages fat build-up.** The same imbalance pushes the liver toward making and storing fat and away from burning it. Over time, regular heavy drinking is the classic cause of alcohol-related fatty liver.
- **It raises lactic acid.** More lactate builds up, which can affect how the kidneys clear uric acid. That's part of why heavy drinking can trigger gout attacks in people prone to them.

None of this is a big deal after one or two drinks in a healthy person. It becomes meaningful with heavy drinking sessions and with drinking that happens most days.

## Step Two: Aldehyde Dehydrogenase Turns Acetaldehyde Into Acetate

Acetaldehyde is the most harmful molecule in this whole chain. It's far more toxic than ethanol itself. It can bind to proteins and DNA, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies acetaldehyde associated with alcohol consumption as a cause of cancer in humans. In the short term, it's linked to flushing, a racing heart, nausea, and headache.

Your body's defense is speed. In most people, aldehyde dehydrogenase (especially the ALDH2 form, which works inside the mitochondria of liver cells) converts acetaldehyde to acetate almost as fast as it's made. So under normal conditions, acetaldehyde levels in the blood stay low.

Problems show up when that second step falls behind the first:

- **Genetics can slow step two.** Some people carry a variant of the ALDH2 gene that makes the enzyme work poorly or barely at all. More on that below.
- **Heavy, fast drinking can overwhelm it.** When large amounts of alcohol arrive quickly, more acetaldehyde can build up, especially in the liver itself.
- **Some medications block it.** Disulfiram (sold as Antabuse) is prescribed specifically to block ALDH. If someone taking it drinks, acetaldehyde builds up and causes intense flushing, nausea, vomiting, and a pounding heart. Several other medicines have been reported to cause similar reactions with alcohol, which is why some prescription labels say not to drink. Ask your pharmacist about anything you take.

Acetaldehyde is one of several suspects in hangovers. It's not the whole story. Dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, low blood sugar, and compounds in darker drinks all seem to play a part, and researchers still debate how much each matters. Our [hangover science hub](/never-hungover/complete-hangover-science-hub-2025) goes through the main theories.

## The Final Step: Acetate Becomes Energy

Acetate leaves the liver and travels through the blood to other tissues. There it's converted into a molecule called acetyl-CoA, the same fuel that comes from breaking down fats and carbohydrates. Cells burn it in their mitochondria for energy, and the end products are carbon dioxide (which you breathe out) and water.

This is where alcohol's calories come from. Pure alcohol provides about 7 calories per gram, which is more than carbohydrate or protein (about 4) and less than fat (about 9). Because the body treats alcohol as a priority to clear, it tends to burn acetate first and put fat-burning on hold while it does. That's one reason regular drinking can make weight management harder, even beyond the calories in the drink itself.

Acetate also has effects of its own. Some research suggests acetate reaching the brain may contribute to the headache and sluggish feeling some people get after drinking, though this is still an area of active study.

## The Backup Pathway: CYP2E1 and the "Trained" Liver

ADH does most of the work at normal levels of drinking. A second system, called the **microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (MEOS)**, steps in more as alcohol levels rise. Its main enzyme is **CYP2E1**, part of the large cytochrome P450 family that also handles many medications.

CYP2E1 matters for three reasons.

**It's inducible.** With regular heavy drinking, the liver makes more CYP2E1. This is a big part of what people call "metabolic tolerance": someone who drinks heavily every day can clear alcohol somewhat faster than they used to. It's not a sign of a healthier liver. It's an adaptation to repeated exposure.

**It makes harmful by-products.** CYP2E1 generates reactive oxygen species, a kind of chemical damage known as oxidative stress. Over years, this contributes to liver inflammation and scarring.

**It handles some medicines too.** The same enzyme processes acetaminophen (Tylenol) into a toxic by-product. A liver primed by heavy drinking produces more of it, which is why acetaminophen and regular heavy drinking are a risky mix. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains that interaction step by step.

A third minor route uses an enzyme called **catalase**, which plays a small role, mostly in the brain. And a tiny fraction of alcohol goes through **non-oxidative** pathways, forming compounds such as ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and phosphatidylethanol (PEth). These are a minuscule share of total metabolism, but they last much longer than alcohol itself, which is why labs use them for tests that detect drinking days or weeks later. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) covers those detection windows.

## How Fast Does the Body Metabolize Alcohol?

For an average adult, the liver clears roughly one standard drink per hour. In blood alcohol terms, an often-quoted average is a drop of about 0.015 g/dL per hour, with a normal range from roughly 0.010 to 0.020 or more depending on the person.

A **standard drink** in the US contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's about:

- 12 ounces of regular beer (around 5% alcohol)
- 5 ounces of wine (around 12% alcohol)
- 1.5 ounces of 80-proof spirits (40% alcohol)

Real drinks often contain more. A strong craft beer, a heavy pour of wine, or a cocktail with two shots can easily be one and a half to two standard drinks, or more. So "one drink an hour" is a rough guide, not a guarantee.

A simple way to picture it: if you reach a blood alcohol level of 0.08% (the legal driving limit in most US states), it will typically take somewhere around five to six hours for it to fall back to zero, and longer if your level was higher. If you finish drinking at 1 a.m. after a heavy night, there's a real chance you're still over the limit at breakfast. Our [blood alcohol calculator](/never-hungover/blood-alcohol-calculator) gives a rough estimate, but no calculator can tell you you're safe to drive.

## What Affects How Quickly You Process Alcohol

Because the liver works at a near-fixed rate, most of what changes how alcohol affects you is about how *high* your blood alcohol gets and how *fast* it gets there, rather than how quickly it's cleared. Here are the factors that matter most.

### Food in your stomach

Eating before or while drinking is the single most useful everyday factor. Food slows the move from stomach to small intestine, where most absorption happens. That means a lower, slower peak and more time for first-pass metabolism. Studies have also found that people clear alcohol somewhat faster after a meal than when fasting, likely because food increases blood flow to the liver. Eating doesn't make you immune to alcohol, but drinking on an empty stomach produces a noticeably sharper rise.

### Body size and body composition

Alcohol spreads through body water, not fat. A larger person with more lean tissue has more water to dilute the same drink, so their blood alcohol level rises less.

### Sex

On average, women reach a higher blood alcohol level than men from the same amount, even at the same body weight. The main reasons are a lower share of body water and, on average, lower stomach ADH activity. Hormonal changes across the menstrual cycle may play a smaller role, though the research on that is mixed.

### Age

As people get older, the share of body water tends to fall, so the same drink tends to produce a higher blood alcohol level. Older adults are also more likely to take medications that interact with alcohol.

### Genetics

Genes are the biggest reason two similar people can respond so differently to the same drink. This gets its own section below.

### Drinking pattern

Regular heavy drinking induces CYP2E1 and can make the liver clear alcohol somewhat faster. Over the long run, though, liver damage does the opposite: a scarred or failing liver clears alcohol and medicines more slowly.

### Medications and health conditions

Some medicines compete for the same enzymes or block ALDH. Liver disease slows clearance. Certain stomach operations, especially some forms of weight-loss surgery, can make alcohol reach the bloodstream much faster, producing higher peaks from smaller amounts. If any of this applies to you, ask your doctor how alcohol fits in.

### Things that don't speed it up

Coffee, cold showers, fresh air, sweating, exercise, and "sleeping it off for an hour" do not meaningfully speed up how fast your liver processes alcohol. Coffee can make you feel more alert, which is risky because you're no less impaired. Drinking water helps with dehydration but doesn't flush alcohol out faster. If you want the full rundown of what does and doesn't help, see our guide on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism). The honest summary is that time is the only reliable sober-up method.

## Genetics: Why Some People Flush and Others Don't

Small differences in the ADH and ALDH genes change how quickly each step runs, and those differences are common.

**The ALDH2 variant (the "Asian flush" gene).** Many people of East Asian descent, including Chinese, Japanese, and Korean heritage, carry a variant called ALDH2*2. It produces an enzyme that works very poorly. A widely cited estimate puts the number of carriers at around 540 million people worldwide, roughly 8% of the global population. When carriers drink, acetaldehyde builds up because step two can't keep up. The result is the **alcohol flush reaction**: facial redness, warmth, a fast heartbeat, and sometimes nausea or headache, often after a single drink.

The flush isn't just cosmetic. Because it signals higher acetaldehyde exposure, research has linked regular drinking in ALDH2-deficient people to a higher risk of esophageal cancer than in people without the variant who drink the same amount. If you flush, the healthiest response is to drink less, not to mask the redness. Antihistamines like Pepcid may reduce the visible redness, but they don't reduce acetaldehyde. Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) explains what helps and what to avoid.

**Fast ADH variants.** Some people carry ADH versions that run step one much faster, such as ADH1B*2, which is also more common in East Asian populations. Faster step one means acetaldehyde is produced more quickly, which can also cause unpleasant reactions. Research has found that people with these fast variants tend, on average, to drink less, probably because drinking feels worse for them.

**Everyone else.** Most people have a mix of variants that produce smaller differences. These small genetic factors, combined with body size, food, and drinking habits, explain why your friend might seem fine after three drinks while you feel flushed or foggy. If you're curious about testing, our guide to [alcohol metabolism genetic testing](/never-hungover/alcohol-metabolism-genetic-testing-complete-personalized-health-guide-2025) explains what consumer tests can and can't tell you.

## What Metabolizing Alcohol Does to Your Body

Even when everything works smoothly, processing alcohol has side effects. Understanding them helps explain how you feel the next day and why habits matter over time.

### In the short term

- **More urine, less water.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, a hormone that helps your kidneys hold on to water. You urinate more and can end up mildly dehydrated, which adds to thirst, dry mouth, and headache.
- **Blood sugar dips.** The NADH imbalance described above can lower blood sugar, especially if you didn't eat.
- **Poorer sleep.** As blood alcohol falls during the night, many people get a rebound effect: lighter sleep, more waking, and less restful sleep in the second half of the night.
- **Acetaldehyde exposure.** Even in people without the flush variant, some acetaldehyde circulates while you drink, and it may contribute to next-day nausea and headache.
- **Inflammation.** Drinking can trigger an immune response, and inflammatory signals are thought to be part of why a hangover feels like being mildly sick.

### Over the long term

When the liver processes large amounts of alcohol regularly, the changes add up. The usual progression is:

1. **Fatty liver.** Fat builds up in liver cells. It's common in people who drink heavily and is often reversible if drinking drops.
2. **Alcohol-related hepatitis.** Inflammation and liver cell damage. This can be serious and needs medical care.
3. **Fibrosis and cirrhosis.** Scar tissue replaces healthy tissue, and the liver gradually loses its ability to work.

Early liver damage often causes no symptoms. If you drink most days, a routine checkup with liver blood tests is a sensible step. For more on the stages and the warning signs, see our [fatty liver disease guide](/never-hungover/fatty-liver-disease-complete-guide-causes-symptoms-natural-treatment-2025).

## When to Talk to a Doctor

For most social drinkers, alcohol metabolism is just something worth understanding. But some signs mean it's time to get checked out:

- **You flush strongly, get hives, or feel very unwell after small amounts.** This could be an enzyme variant, an intolerance, or a reaction to something in the drink, and it's worth discussing with a doctor.
- **You take regular medication.** Many medicines share liver enzymes with alcohol or have specific alcohol warnings. A pharmacist can check your list quickly.
- **You notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, pain under your right ribs, swelling in your belly or legs, or easy bruising.** These can be signs of liver trouble and need prompt medical attention.
- **You find you need more alcohol to feel the same effect, or you feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you go without.** Rising tolerance and feeling unwell when you stop can mean your body has adapted to regular alcohol. Stopping suddenly after heavy daily drinking can be dangerous, so talk to a doctor before cutting back sharply. They can help you do it safely.

And again: confusion, unresponsiveness, vomiting while drowsy, seizures, or slow or irregular breathing after drinking are a medical emergency. Call 911. Keep the person on their side and don't leave them alone.

## Practical Takeaways for a Night Out

Knowing how alcohol is metabolized makes the usual advice make sense:

- **Pace to roughly one standard drink per hour or slower.** That keeps you close to the rate your liver can actually clear, rather than stacking alcohol up in your blood.
- **Eat a real meal before you start.** It lowers your peak and gives first-pass metabolism a chance to work.
- **Alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink.** It slows your pace and offsets some of the fluid loss.
- **Count real drinks, not glasses.** Big pours and strong beers count as more than one.
- **Don't drive the next morning on a guess.** If you drank heavily late at night, alcohol may still be in your blood.
- **If you flush, take it seriously.** It's your body telling you acetaldehyde is building up.
- **Don't take acetaminophen to "pre-empt" a hangover.** Your liver is already busy, and the two compete for the same machinery.

For a fuller plan, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Where Does DHM Fit In?

Dihydromyricetin (DHM) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis) that's sold as a hangover supplement. Much of the interest in it comes from animal research. In a 2012 study in rats published in the Journal of Neuroscience, DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal, apparently by acting on GABA receptors in the brain. Later work in mice has reported that DHM may increase the activity of the alcohol-processing enzymes and reduce liver fat build-up from alcohol.

It's important to be clear about the limits. Most of this evidence comes from animals, and human data is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM lets you drink more safely, lowers your blood alcohol fast enough to drive, or protects people with the ALDH2 flush variant from acetaldehyde. It does not replace pacing, food, water, and time.

If you want to try it alongside sensible habits, two commonly chosen options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with L-cysteine and other ingredients, and the simpler, lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [liver supplement guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) compares DHM with other options. If you take prescription medication or have a liver condition, check with your doctor before starting any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Your liver metabolizes alcohol in two main steps: alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol into toxic acetaldehyde, and aldehyde dehydrogenase turns that into harmless acetate, which the body burns for energy. A backup system (CYP2E1) takes on more work as drinking gets heavier and more regular. The whole process runs at a near-fixed pace, roughly one standard drink an hour, so the only things you can really control are how much you drink, how fast, and whether you've eaten. Genetics, sex, body size, age, and medications explain most of the differences between people. Nothing on the market speeds the liver up in a meaningful way, and time remains the only reliable way to sober up.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How is alcohol metabolized in the body?**

Mostly in the liver, in two main steps. The enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethanol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound. A second enzyme, aldehyde dehydrogenase (mainly ALDH2), converts acetaldehyde into acetate. Acetate then travels to other tissues and is broken down into carbon dioxide and water. A small amount of alcohol, usually under 10%, leaves the body unchanged through breath, urine, and sweat.

**Where is alcohol metabolized?**

The liver handles the large majority, often estimated at 90% or more. The stomach lining breaks down a small amount before absorption (part of first-pass metabolism), and minor pathways exist in other tissues, including the brain. A few percent is exhaled, which is why breath tests work.

**How long does it take to metabolize one drink?**

For an average adult, roughly one hour per standard drink (about 14 grams of alcohol, such as a 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot). The real time varies with body size, sex, genetics, liver health, and food. Larger pours and stronger drinks take longer to clear.

**Can you speed up alcohol metabolism?**

Not meaningfully. Coffee, cold showers, exercise, and drinking water don't make your liver clear alcohol faster. Eating before drinking lowers your peak level and may slightly increase clearance, but time is the only reliable way to sober up.

**Why do some people get red when they drink?**

Many people, especially of East Asian descent, carry a variant of the ALDH2 gene that makes the enzyme work poorly. Acetaldehyde builds up instead of being converted to acetate, causing facial flushing, a fast heartbeat, and sometimes nausea. The flush signals higher exposure to a toxic compound, so drinking less is the healthiest response.

**Why do women feel the effects of alcohol more than men?**

On average, women have a lower share of body water and less alcohol dehydrogenase activity in the stomach. Both lead to a higher blood alcohol level from the same amount of alcohol, even at the same body weight.

**Does tolerance mean your liver processes alcohol faster?**

Partly. Regular heavy drinking increases an enzyme called CYP2E1, so the liver can clear alcohol somewhat faster. But much of tolerance is the brain adapting, so you feel less impaired than you really are. Neither type is a sign of good health, and rising tolerance is worth discussing with a doctor.

**Does DHM help your body metabolize alcohol?**

Animal studies suggest DHM may increase the activity of alcohol-processing enzymes and reduce some effects of alcohol, but human evidence is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers blood alcohol fast enough to drive or makes heavy drinking safe. Pacing, food, water, and time still matter most.
